title: Jim Crow, Du Bois, the NAACP and the Great Migration
welcome_lead: From Plessy to the New Deal: organising against segregation.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Plessy 1896, Washington vs Du Bois, the NAACP 1909 and the Great Migration.
final_note: You can chart the strategies adopted by African Americans before 1954.

walkthroughs.body_html: Mississippi (1890) and others used poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses to disenfranchise black voters. Plessy v Ferguson (1896) blessed segregation. Lynchings averaged over 100 per year in the 1890s. Ida B. Wells campaigned against lynching from 1892.

Booker T Washington's Atlanta Compromise (1895) accepted segregation in return for economic uplift. Du Bois's Niagara Movement (1905) and his role at the NAACP (1909) prioritised legal rights and the 'Talented Tenth'. The NAACP achieved early wins: Guinn v United States (1915) struck down grandfather clauses.

WWI labour demand and the Great Migration transformed cities. Race riots erupted in 1919 (Red Summer) and Tulsa (1921). Marcus Garvey's UNIA peaked 1919-23. The Harlem Renaissance, with Hughes, Hurston and Ellington, showcased cultural achievement. New Deal programmes were mixed: AAA hurt sharecroppers; Eleanor Roosevelt and the 'Black Cabinet' offered new access; the 1941 March on Washington Movement led to FDR's Executive Order 8802 banning defence-industry discrimination.

mcqs.q: What did Brown v Board of Education decide in 1954?
options: The Supreme Court ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v Ferguson and beginning legal dismantling of school segregation.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Brown v Board of Education immediately desegregated all schools in America.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.

mcqs.q: How was the US civil rights movement achieved?
options: Martin Luther King's 'I Have a Dream' speech ended segregation.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Through decades of mass organising — NAACP legal work, grassroots campaigns, sit-ins, freedom rides — alongside leaders like King and Malcolm X.

mcqs.q: How did Malcolm X's approach differ from MLK's?
options: Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Malcolm X advocated violent terrorism against white Americans.
MLK preached nonviolent integration; Malcolm X (until 1964) advocated black self-defence, separatism, and rejected integration as a goal — though both shifted positions over time.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.
